title: Gauss's Law
summary: Electric flux measures how much field passes through a surface, $\Phi = EA\cos\theta$. Gauss's law says the net flux through any closed surface equals the enclosed charge over $\varepsilon_0$: $\Phi = \dfrac{Q_{enc}}{\varepsilon_0}$. With enough symmetry this gives the field quickly. (University Physics Vol. 2, Ch. 6.)

concept_sections.heading: Electric flux
concept_sections.explanation: Flux is field times the area it passes through, counting only the perpendicular part: $\Phi = EA\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{E}$ and the surface's normal. When the field is perpendicular to the surface, $\Phi = EA$; when parallel, $\Phi = 0$. Units are N·m$^2$/C.
math_steps: Flux counts field crossing an area: $\Phi = EA\cos\theta$.
$\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{E}$ and the surface's normal (the arrow sticking straight out).
Perpendicular field ($\theta=0$): $\Phi = EA$ (maximum). Field grazing the surface ($\theta=90^\circ$): $\Phi = 0$.
Units are N·m$^2$/C.

figure.caption: Only the perpendicular part of $\vec{E}$ counts: $\Phi=EA\cos\theta$.

concept_sections.heading: Gauss's law
concept_sections.explanation: For any closed surface, the total flux out equals the charge enclosed divided by $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}$ F/m: $\Phi = \dfrac{Q_{enc}}{\varepsilon_0}$. Charges outside the surface contribute zero net flux — their field lines enter and leave. Only enclosed charge counts.
math_steps: Draw a closed surface. Add up the flux poking out through all of it.
Gauss's law: $\Phi = \dfrac{Q_{enc}}{\varepsilon_0}$, with $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}$ F/m.
Charges outside contribute zero net flux — their lines enter one side and leave the other.
Only the charge enclosed by the surface matters.

figure.caption: Flux out of a closed surface = enclosed charge / $\varepsilon_0$. Outside charge adds nothing.

concept_sections.heading: Using symmetry
concept_sections.explanation: Gauss's law is most powerful when the field is constant over a chosen 'Gaussian surface.' Use a sphere for point/spherical charge, a cylinder for a line/wire, and a pillbox for a plane. Then $E$ comes out of the flux integral and you solve $E\,A = Q_{enc}/\varepsilon_0$ for $E$.
math_steps: Pick a Gaussian surface matching the symmetry: sphere for a point, cylinder for a line, pillbox for a sheet.
On that surface $E$ is constant and perpendicular, so $\Phi = E\,A$.
Set it equal to the enclosed charge term: $E\,A = Q_{enc}/\varepsilon_0$.
Solve for $E$ — the hard integral disappears.

figure.caption: A cylinder fits a line charge: solve $E\,A=Q_{enc}/\varepsilon_0$ for $E$.

concept_sections.heading: Conductors
concept_sections.explanation: In electrostatic equilibrium the field inside a conductor is zero, so any net charge sits on its surface. A Gaussian surface just inside the conductor encloses no net charge. This is why a hollow conductor shields its interior — the basis of the Faraday cage.
math_steps: In equilibrium, charges in a conductor rearrange until the inside field is zero.
A Gaussian surface just inside the metal encloses no net charge $\Rightarrow$ $\Phi=0 \Rightarrow E=0$.
So any net charge must sit on the outer surface.
A hollow conductor therefore shields its interior — a Faraday cage.

figure.caption: Charge sits on the surface; the field inside a conductor is zero.

concept_sections.heading: Standard results
concept_sections.explanation: Gauss's law gives clean formulas: infinite sheet of charge $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$; just outside a conductor $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$; infinite line of charge $E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r} = \dfrac{2k\lambda}{r}$; outside a spherical charge the field is the same as a point charge at the center.
math_steps: Infinite sheet: $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$ (field is uniform, both sides).
Just outside a conductor: $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$ (no factor of 2).
Infinite line: $E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r} = \dfrac{2k\lambda}{r}$ (falls off as $1/r$).
Outside a charged sphere: same as a point charge $k Q/r^2$ at the center.

figure.caption: From outside, a charged sphere acts like a point charge at its center.

real_world_examples.title: Safe inside a car during lightning
real_world_examples.scenario: A car struck by lightning protects the people inside.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The metal shell is a conductor, so by Gauss's law the field (and enclosed charge) inside is zero — a Faraday cage. Charge stays on the outer surface.
real_world_examples.detail: The steel body is a conductor. When lightning hits, the charge races around the outer shell and the field inside stays zero (Gauss's law). The people inside are in a Faraday cage — the rubber tires are not what saves you.

figure.caption: Lightning charge stays on the shell; the field inside the car is zero.

real_world_examples.title: Coaxial cable shielding
real_world_examples.scenario: TV/antenna cables have a braided outer conductor.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: A cylindrical Gaussian surface shows the outer conductor cancels external fields, keeping the signal on the inner wire clean.
real_world_examples.detail: The signal travels on the inner wire. The braided outer conductor is a cylindrical shield: by Gauss's law it cancels outside fields, so noise never reaches the inner conductor.

figure.caption: The outer conductor forms a Gaussian shield around the signal wire.

real_world_examples.title: Microwave oven door mesh
real_world_examples.scenario: The door has a metal screen you can see through.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The conducting mesh acts as a Gaussian shield: enclosed field is blocked, keeping microwaves in while letting light out.
real_world_examples.detail: The holes in the metal screen are far smaller than the microwave wavelength (~12 cm), so the mesh acts as a continuous conductor for microwaves — a Gaussian shield that keeps them in — while visible light (tiny wavelength) passes through.

figure.caption: The conducting mesh blocks microwaves but lets light through.

problems.prompt: A uniform field $E = 500$ N/C passes perpendicular through a flat area $A = 2.0\ \text{m}^2$. Find the flux.
The same field $E = 500$ N/C and area $A = 2.0\ \text{m}^2$, but now the field makes $60^\circ$ with the surface normal. Find the flux.
The net flux out of a closed surface is $1.13\times10^{5}$ N·m$^2$/C. How much charge is enclosed?
Find the field from an infinite sheet with surface charge density $\sigma = 8.85\times10^{-9}\ \text{C/m}^2$.
problems.hint: Use the infinite-sheet result with the factor of 2.

problems.prompt: Just outside a charged conductor the surface density is $\sigma = 1.77\times10^{-8}\ \text{C/m}^2$. Find the field there.
problems.hint: At a conductor's surface there is no factor of 2.

problems.prompt: A charge of $5.0\ \mu\text{C}$ is spread uniformly on a sphere. Find the field $0.20$ m outside its center.
solution_steps: Outside a spherical charge the field equals a point charge at the center.
problems.hint: Gauss's law makes the sphere look like a point charge from outside.

problems.prompt: A charge sits inside a hollow metal sphere. What is the electric field within the metal itself (in equilibrium)?
solution_steps: A Gaussian surface inside the metal encloses no net charge, so the field is zero.
problems.hint: Think about the field inside conducting material.

problems.prompt: An infinite line carries $\lambda = 3.0\ \mu\text{C/m}$. Find the field $0.10$ m away.
problems.hint: Use a cylindrical Gaussian surface; the line-charge field falls off as $1/r$.

problems.prompt: A point charge $q = 6.0$ nC sits at the center of a cube. Find the flux through one face.
solution_steps: By symmetry each of the 6 faces gets an equal share.
problems.hint: By symmetry the total flux splits equally among the six faces.

problems.prompt: Inside a closed surface are charges $+2\ \mu\text{C}$, $+3\ \mu\text{C}$, and $-1\ \mu\text{C}$; a $+10\ \mu\text{C}$ charge sits just outside. Find the net flux through the surface.
solution_steps: Only enclosed charge counts: $Q_{enc} = 2+3-1 = 4\ \mu\text{C}$ (the outside $10\ \mu$C contributes zero).
problems.hint: External charges add no net flux — sum only the enclosed charge.

flux.plain: How much of something flows through an area — here, how much electric field pokes through a surface.
flux.in_class: Electric flux $\Phi = EA\cos\theta$, counting only the part of $\vec{E}$ perpendicular to the surface. Units N·m$^2$/C.

Gauss's law.plain: A shortcut connecting the field poking out of a closed surface to the charge trapped inside it.
Gauss's law.in_class: $\Phi = Q_{enc}/\varepsilon_0$: net flux through any closed surface equals the enclosed charge over $\varepsilon_0$.

Gaussian surface.plain: An imaginary closed surface you draw in just the right shape to make the math easy.
Gaussian surface.in_class: A chosen closed surface (sphere, cylinder, or pillbox) matched to the symmetry so $E$ is constant on it and pulls out of the flux integral.

symmetry.plain: When something looks the same from different directions, so the answer can't favor one direction.
symmetry.in_class: The property that lets $E$ be constant over the Gaussian surface, turning Gauss's law into $E\,A = Q_{enc}/\varepsilon_0$.

conductor.plain: A material whose charges move freely, like metal.
conductor.in_class: In electrostatic equilibrium $\vec{E}=0$ inside it; net charge lives on the surface — the basis of shielding (Faraday cage).

Faraday cage.plain: A metal shell that keeps electric fields out of whatever is inside it.
Faraday cage.in_class: A hollow conductor: a Gaussian surface just inside encloses no net charge, so the interior field is zero.
